overview: The United States provides food, medicine, vaccines, and medical supplies to people in other countries through foreign aid programs, and some of these goods have expired or spoiled in storage before reaching anyone. This bill, the Saving Lives and Taxpayer Dollars Act, would require the State Department to send Congress a yearly report, through 2030, on any aid products that were destroyed after spoiling, expiring, or being contaminated despite reasonable efforts to prevent it. Each report would explain what was done to prevent the waste, why the goods couldn't be delivered (including any laws in the recipient country that got in the way), where they were meant to go, what they were worth, and what it cost to destroy them. As of July 27, 2026, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee had approved an amended version and it was awaiting a vote by the full Senate.
for: Supporters say regular public reporting on wasted aid will help Congress spot problems and push agencies to get lifesaving supplies to people before they go bad.
against: Critics say the committee's version only requires reports, dropping language from the original bill that would have required agencies to actually deliver or donate the goods before they expire.
